question: A 45-year-old hypertensive woman presents with sudden onset severe headache and complete right-sided CN III palsy including a fixed, dilated pupil. Which single feature most reliably differentiates this from a diabetic (medical) CN III palsy?

answers.text: Complete ptosis with exotropia and hypotropia of the affected eye

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both medical and surgical CN III palsies can cause complete ptosis and a 'down and out' deviation. This pattern alone does not distinguish the two.

answers.text: Pupil involvement — fixed, dilated pupil unresponsive to light

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The pupillomotor fibres run peripherally in CN III and are compressed first by an expanding aneurysm (posterior communicating artery). Diabetic ischaemia spares these peripheral fibres, giving a 'pupil-sparing' palsy. A fixed dilated pupil mandates urgent neuroimaging.
Diplopia on upgaze is expected in any CN III palsy affecting the superior rectus. It does not distinguish surgical from medical aetiology.

answers.text: Onset over several days rather than hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Diabetic CN III palsy can also present acutely. Onset speed is not a reliable distinguishing feature; pupil involvement is the critical differentiator.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: the pupillomotor fibres lie on the peripheral surface of CN III and are compressed early by an aneurysm. A fixed dilated pupil with CN III palsy is a neurosurgical emergency.
Well done. Pupil involvement = surgical (aneurysm) until proven otherwise. Act fast — order CT/CTA and call neurosurgery.
